Cheat Sheet: the whole midterm on one page

This is everything the old midterm, both problem sets, and the TA session test. Each row is one idea: the econ on top, plain English underneath, and pills that jump to the worked solution (green) or the original page (outlined). If you can explain every row out loud, you are ready.

Test game plan (format of the old midterm: T/F with justification, then multi-part problems, 100 pts).

  • No credit without explanation. The header of the exam says it. A bare True or False, or a number with no setup, scores zero: always write the one-line reason.
  • Read the clues. Fee and crowded mean private good; free and empty mean public good. The words in the problem ARE the classification.
  • Population weights. Whenever types have different headcounts (5, 10, 10), every sum, average, and welfare loss carries those weights. Forgetting the 5/10/10 is the top lost-points move.
  • Negative demands stay in. If a type's desired quantity comes out negative (like $-1$), keep it in the average. Do not set it to zero.

Spot the good type from the story

EconExcludable (a fee can keep you out) + rival (crowded: my use blocks yours) = private good. Non-excludable + non-rival (empty park, broadcasting) = public good.
Plain English"Must pay a fee, always crowded" and "no fee, almost always empty" are not flavor text: they are the whole question. Classify first, then aggregate.

Private good: add quantities (horizontal sum)

EconAt each price, $Q = Q_x + Q_y$. Midterm: $Q = (200-2P) + (200-4P) = 400 - 6P$. Full credit detail: above \$50 only X buys, so the curve kinks at $P=50$.
Plain EnglishEveryone faces the same price and each person takes home their own units, so you count up the total units bought.

Public good: add willingness to pay (vertical sum)

EconInvert first: $P_x = 100 - \tfrac12 Q$, $P_y = 50 - \tfrac14 Q$. Then $P = P_x + P_y = 150 - \tfrac34 Q$, i.e. $Q = 200 - \tfrac43 P$.
Plain EnglishEveryone consumes the same units together, so at each quantity you stack what each person would pay for one more unit.

Samuelson condition: $\sum MB_i = MC$

EconEfficient public-good level: the summed marginal benefits across everyone equal marginal cost. Rock concerts: $SMB(3) = 100+75+50+200 = 425 = MC$, so $Q^*=3$.
Plain EnglishProvide another unit as long as the group's combined value for it beats what it costs. This is also your efficiency CHECK for any quantity someone hands you.

Lindahl prices: pay your own MB

EconEach person's personalized price equals their own $MB$ at $Q^*$; the prices sum to $MC$. With constant $MC$, total payment $= Q^* \times MB_i$: Olive \$300, Peter \$225, Austin \$150, others \$600.
Plain EnglishEveryone gets the same quantity but pays a different price matched to how much they care. Nobody wants to change $Q$, so it is an equilibrium and it is efficient.

Economies of scale and optimal community size

Econ$AC(n) = TC(n)/n$. Economies of scale: $AC$ falling in $n$. Optimal size: $n^* = \arg\min AC(n)$, so set $\partial AC/\partial n = 0$. PS2: per-person cost $G^2 + (4-N)^2 G$ is smallest at $N=4$.
Plain EnglishFind the town size where the per-resident bill for the same service is cheapest. Too few people: nobody to split the bill with. Too many: congestion costs creep in.

Decentralization theorem (know the conditions!)

EconOates: with no spillovers and no economies of scale, local provision of the Pareto-efficient local level is weakly better than any uniform central level; strictly better when preferences differ. Checklist for centralizing: spillovers, scale economies, mobility of the tax base, admin costs. For decentralizing: variety in demand, voting with feet.
Plain EnglishTowns that pick their own level beat one-size-fits-all, PROVIDED nothing leaks across borders and bigger is not cheaper. MT 1a is False precisely because exhausting scale economies does not speak to spillovers or preferences.

Property tax as a benefit tax; the free-rider temptation

EconWith identical houses (zoning), pay $=$ get: A pays $0.04 \times 500{,}000 = \$20{,}000$ for \$20,000 schools; B pays \$7,000 for \$7,000. The temptation: a below-average-value house in a high-spending district pays less than it gets.
Plain EnglishZoning makes the property tax work like a price tag: you buy the school package your house pays for. Kill the zoning and the smart move is a small house among big ones. Careful on 3b: the key says you cannot be SURE they move (see the trap in Tab 3).

Capitalization: taxes get priced into the house

EconPrice $=$ PV of what the house delivers: $P = V + \dfrac{G - T}{r}$. Higher property tax, services fixed $\Rightarrow$ $P$ falls. MT 1b is False: the statement has the sign backwards.
Plain EnglishA house bundled with bigger future tax bills sells for less, not more. A house bundled with a sweet deal (schools worth more than its taxes) sells at a premium: the free ride is sold to you up front.

Mixed district: tax the average house value

EconRevenue per pupil $= t \times \bar V$. Two big (\$500k) per small (\$200k): $\bar V = \tfrac{2(500)+1(200)}{3} = \$400$k, so $t = \tfrac{20{,}000}{400{,}000} = 5\%$.
Plain EnglishOne pupil per house means spending per pupil is just the tax collected per house on average. Weight the house values by how many there are, then divide the spending target by that average.

Capitalized prices by indifference (the key's method)

EconTotal cost of owning $=$ price $+ \dfrac{\text{annual tax}}{r}$, and the tax is levied on the MARKET price, so it collapses: $500{,}000 + \tfrac{20{,}000}{0.05} = 2P_{BH}$, giving $P_{BH} = \$450$k. Small: $600{,}000 = 2P_{SH}$, so $P_{SH} = \$300$k.
Plain EnglishSet "cost of the big house here" equal to "cost of the big house in district A" and solve. The price shows up on both sides because a pricier house also pays more tax: that is why the premium is \$100k, not \$200k.

Hamilton 1975: capitalization vs more zoned towns

EconHamilton: solving the free-rider problem with zoning alone needs a separate homogeneous community per house-type/spending combo. With full capitalization, mixed districts are stable: the small house's fiscal surplus is priced in, so no one gains by moving.
Plain EnglishYou do not need a town for every taste if house prices do the work: the \$300k small house already charges you the present value of the free ride at closing.

Barzel welfare loss: $\Delta W_i = \dfrac{(Q_i - Q_0)^2}{2|b_i|}$

EconFor demand $Q_i = a_i + b_i P$, forcing $Q_0$ instead of the desired $Q_i$ costs a triangle $\tfrac{1}{2|b_i|}(Q_i - Q_0)^2$. Same slopes $\Rightarrow$ the loss-minimizing uniform $Q^*$ is the population-weighted AVERAGE of desired quantities.
Plain EnglishThe farther the forced quantity sits from what you wanted, the worse (and it grows with the square of the distance). The best compromise for the whole town is the average wish, counting heads.

District division: group similar demands

EconMidterm: desired $Q$'s at $P=2$ are $2, -1, 5$. Proposal 1 $\{1\},\{2,3\}$: $DWL = 45$. Proposal 2 $\{1,2\},\{3\}$: $DWL = \tfrac{15}{2}$. Proposal 2 wins: it isolates the outlier type 3 and pairs the two closest types.
Plain EnglishRedistricting works when the people inside each district want similar amounts: that is Tiebout sorting in miniature. Compare proposals by computing each district's average, then summing the weighted squared gaps.

Numbers to know cold.

  • Park demands: $Q_x = 200 - 2P_x$, $Q_y = 200 - 4P_y$ → private $Q = \mathbf{400 - 6P}$, public $P = \mathbf{150 - \tfrac34 Q}$.
  • School districts: A $= \$500$k at $4\% = \$\mathbf{20{,}000}$; B $= \$200$k at $3.5\% = \$7{,}000$, then at $10\% = \$20{,}000$. Mixed base $\bar V = \$\mathbf{400}$k $\Rightarrow t = \mathbf{5\%}$. Capitalized: $P_{BH} = \$\mathbf{450}$k, $P_{SH} = \$\mathbf{300}$k at $r = 5\%$. Cost of any big house $= \$900$k; any small house $= \$600$k.
  • Deadweight loss (MT 4): tax prices $2, 1, 3$ → desired $\mathbf{2, 1, 3}$. Equal shares: $P = \tfrac{50}{25} = 2$ → desired $\mathbf{2, -1, 5}$; optimum $Q^* = \mathbf{2}$; $\sum MB = \mathbf{50} = MC$; proposals: $\mathbf{45}$ vs $\mathbf{7.5}$.
  • Rock concerts: vertical sums $\mathbf{975, 700, 425, 250}$; $MC = 425 \Rightarrow Q^* = \mathbf{3}$; Lindahl payments $\mathbf{300, 225, 150, 600}$ (sum $= 1275 = 425 \times 3$).
  • Picnic area (PS1 5): $MB$s $\tfrac{5}{4G}$ and $\tfrac{59}{4G}$, $MC = G$ → $G^* = \mathbf{4}$; president alone picks $G = \tfrac{\sqrt 5}{2} \approx 1.12$ (underprovision).
  • PS2 community size: optimal $N = \mathbf{4}$; with 2 old $+$ 2 young, $\sum MRS = 8 = MC \Rightarrow G^* = \mathbf{1}$.
  • Top five state and local revenue sources (MT 5): intergovernmental transfers from the federal government, property taxes, sales taxes, individual income taxes, charges and user fees.

Sources: the old midterm and its answer key, Problem Sets 1 and 2, and TA Session 2 notes (Oct 9). Every pill jumps to the worked solution or the original page.

Aggregation and efficiency

Private good: horizontal sum

$Q^{agg}(P) = \sum_i Q_i(P)$

  • Add QUANTITIES at each price.
  • Respect choke prices: drop a person once $P$ exceeds their intercept (kink!).
  • MT 2a: $Q = 400 - 6P$ for $P \le 50$; $Q = 200 - 2P$ for $50 < P \le 100$.

Public good: vertical sum

$P^{agg}(Q) = \sum_i P_i(Q) = \sum_i MB_i(Q)$

  • Invert each demand first, then add PRICES at each quantity.
  • MT 2b: $P = (100 - \tfrac12 Q) + (50 - \tfrac14 Q) = 150 - \tfrac34 Q$.

Samuelson condition

$\sum_i MB_i(Q^*) = MC(Q^*)$

  • Efficient provision of a public good; also the CHECK for Pareto efficiency of a proposed $Q$.
  • With populations: $\sum_t n_t \, MB_t(Q^*) = MC$.

Lindahl prices

$p_i = MB_i(Q^*)$, with $\sum_i p_i = MC$

  • Personalized per-unit prices; everyone demands the same $Q^*$.
  • Constant $MC$ shortcut (TA): total payment $= Q^* \cdot MB_i(Q^*)$.

MB from a table

$SMB(Q) = $ sum of the column at $Q$

  • Rock concerts: add Olive, Peter, Austin, and All Others at each quantity.
  • Efficient $Q^*$: the quantity where the summed column equals $MC$.

Clubs and fiscal federalism

Average cost and optimal community size

$AC(n) = \dfrac{TC(n)}{n}, \qquad n^* = \arg\min_n AC(n)$

  • Economies of scale: $AC$ decreasing in $n$.
  • PS2: per-person cost $G^2 + (4-N)^2 G$ is minimized at $N^* = 4$.

Decentralization theorem (Oates)

No spillovers $+$ no scale economies $\Rightarrow$ local $\succeq$ uniform central

  • Strictly better when preferences are heterogeneous.
  • Both conditions must be checked before invoking it (MT 1a!).

MRS version of Samuelson

$\sum_i MRS^i_{G,x} = MC_G$

  • $MRS = MU_G / MU_x$; private good is the numeraire.
  • PS2: old $MRS = 1$, young $MRS = 3$; $2(1) + 2(3) = 8 = MC(G) \Rightarrow G^* = 1$.

Property taxes and capitalization

Tax bill and per-pupil spending

$T = t \times V, \qquad G = t \times \bar V$

  • One pupil per house: spending per pupil $=$ average tax per house.
  • Mixed district: $\bar V = \tfrac{2(500\text{k}) + 200\text{k}}{3} = 400$k $\Rightarrow t = 5\%$.

Capitalization (perpetuity)

$P = V + \dfrac{G - T}{r}$

  • Annual fiscal surplus or deficit, divided by $r$, lands in the price.
  • Sign on MT 1b: tax up, services fixed $\Rightarrow$ price DOWN.

Indifference pricing (the key's setup)

$P_1 + \dfrac{t_1 P_1}{r} = P_2 + \dfrac{t_2 P_2}{r}$

  • Equal total cost of the same house type across districts; schools equal, so they cancel.
  • With $t = r = 5\%$ the mixed side collapses to $2P$: $900\text{k} = 2P_{BH}$, $600\text{k} = 2P_{SH}$.

Benefit-tax equilibrium

pay $=$ get for every house, everywhere

  • MT 3f: all districts spend \$20k; costs \$900k (big) and \$600k (small) in every district; no one moves.
  • Hamilton (MT 3g): capitalization makes mixed districts stable without extra zoned towns.

Welfare loss (Barzel)

Welfare loss triangle

$\Delta W_i = \dfrac{(Q_i - Q_0)^2}{2|b_i|}$

  • Triangle form: $\tfrac12 (Q_i - Q_0)\,(P_i(Q_0) - P_0)$.
  • $Q_i$ = desired at the common price; $Q_0$ = what the district imposes.
  • MT slope $b = -2$: coefficient $\tfrac14$. TA slope $b = -3$: coefficient $\tfrac16$.

Averaging rule (same slopes)

$Q^* = \dfrac{\sum_t n_t Q_t}{\sum_t n_t}$

  • The loss-minimizing uniform quantity is the population-weighted mean of desired quantities.
  • Keep negative $Q_t$ in the average!

MB from linear demand

$Q = a + bP \;\Rightarrow\; MB(Q) = \dfrac{Q - a}{b} = \dfrac{a - Q}{|b|}$

  • Plug $Q^*$ in per type, weight by headcount, compare to $MC$: that is the Pareto check.
  • MT 4c: $5(2) + 10(\tfrac12) + 10(\tfrac72) = 50 = MC$. ✓

District comparison recipe

$DWL = \sum_t n_t \dfrac{(Q_t - Q^*_{D(t)})^2}{2|b|}$

  • Per proposal: average within each district, then sum weighted squared gaps.
  • MT 4d: 45 vs 7.5; TA exercise: 18 vs 20. Smaller wins.

1

Public vs private goods: aggregation, Samuelson, Lindahl

One skill decides this whole topic: read the story, classify the good, then aggregate the right way. Private goods share a price (add the $Q$'s). Public goods share a quantity (add the $P$'s). Play with the explorer below until both directions feel obvious.

Play first

Aggregation explorer: the midterm's park demands

$Q_x = 200 - 2P_x$ and $Q_y = 200 - 4P_y$, drawn from the actual equations. Switch modes and drag the slider.

Classify from the clues

Excludable?Rival?Aggregate by
Private good (fee + crowded)Yes: a fee keeps you outYes: crowded means my use blocks yoursHorizontal: $Q = \sum Q_i$ at each $P$
Public good (free + empty)No: no fee chargedNo: empty means my use costs you nothingVertical: $P = \sum MB_i$ at each $Q$

Memory hook: private goods share a price (sum the $Q$'s); public goods share a quantity (sum the $P$'s).

MT 2a

Park with a fee, always crowded: private good

Two individuals, X and Y, have inverse demand curves for a community park: $Q_x = 200 - 2P_x$ and $Q_y = 200 - 4P_y$. Everyone must pay a fee to enter and the park is always crowded. Calculate the aggregate demand.
Givens
  • $Q_x = 200 - 2P_x$, $Q_y = 200 - 4P_y$
  • Fee $\Rightarrow$ excludable; crowded $\Rightarrow$ rival $\Rightarrow$ private good
Add quantities at each common price
$$Q = Q_x + Q_y = (200 - 2P) + (200 - 4P) = 400 - 6P$$
Full-credit detail: the kink
Y's choke price is $P = 50$ and X's is $P = 100$, so for $50 < P \le 100$ only X buys: $Q = 200 - 2P$ there, and $Q = 400 - 6P$ for $P \le 50$. The kink sits at $(Q, P) = (100, 50)$.
Answer $Q = 400 - 6P$ (key's answer), with the kink at $P = 50$ noted
Variation · try it yourself
Same park, but demands are $Q_x = 120 - 2P$ and $Q_y = 120 - 3P$. Aggregate demand if it is a private good?
Horizontal sum
$Q = 240 - 5P$ for $P \le 40$ (Y's choke price); $Q = 120 - 2P$ for $40 < P \le 60$.
MT 2b

No fee, almost always empty: public good

Same two demands, but no fee is charged and the park is almost always empty. Calculate the aggregate demand.
Givens
  • No fee $\Rightarrow$ non-excludable; empty $\Rightarrow$ non-rival $\Rightarrow$ public good
  • Everyone consumes the SAME $Q$, so invert first
Invert each demand
$$Q_x = 200 - 2P_x \Rightarrow P_x = 100 - \tfrac12 Q \qquad Q_y = 200 - 4P_y \Rightarrow P_y = 50 - \tfrac14 Q$$
Add willingness to pay at each quantity
$$P = P_x + P_y = 150 - \tfrac34 Q \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Q = 200 - \tfrac43 P$$
Check
Both individual curves hit $P_i = 0$ at exactly $Q = 200$, so the aggregate is one straight line from $(0, 150)$ to $(200, 0)$: no kink here.
Answer $P = 150 - \tfrac34 Q$ (equivalently $Q = 200 - \tfrac43 P$)
PS1 3

Alex and Chris: same curves, both regimes

$P_A = 100 - \tfrac12 Q_A$, $P_C = 200 - Q_C$, and $MC = \tfrac14 Q$. (a) If the good is private, find the competitive equilibrium price and quantity. Is it efficient? (b) If the good is public, what do price and quantity look like under efficient provision?
Givens
  • Demands (inverse): $P_A = 100 - \tfrac12 Q_A$, $P_C = 200 - Q_C$; so $Q_A = 200 - 2P$, $Q_C = 200 - P$
  • Supply: $MC = \tfrac14 Q$, i.e. $Q^s = 4P$
(a) Private: horizontal sum, then supply = demand
$$Q^d = Q_A + Q_C = 400 - 3P \ (P \le 100) \qquad 4P = 400 - 3P \Rightarrow P^* = \tfrac{400}{7} \approx 57.14,\ Q^* = \tfrac{1600}{7} \approx 228.57$$ Efficient: yes. In a competitive market each buyer sets own $MB = P = MC$, and there are no externalities, so the First Welfare Theorem applies.
(b) Public: vertical sum, then Samuelson
$$SMB = \left(100 - \tfrac12 Q\right) + (200 - Q) = 300 - \tfrac32 Q \qquad 300 - \tfrac32 Q = \tfrac14 Q \Rightarrow Q^* = \tfrac{1200}{7} \approx 171.43$$ The "price" is the summed marginal benefit at $Q^*$: $MC = \tfrac14 \cdot \tfrac{1200}{7} = \tfrac{300}{7} \approx 42.86$, split as personalized prices $P_A = \tfrac{100}{7} \approx 14.29$ and $P_C = \tfrac{200}{7} \approx 28.57$.
Answer (a) $P \approx 57.14$, $Q \approx 228.57$, efficient. (b) $Q \approx 171.43$ with total marginal value $\approx 42.86$ split by individual MBs.
PS1 4

Rock concerts: tables, Samuelson, Lindahl

Marginal benefits per summer concert: Olive 150/125/100/75, Peter 125/100/75/50, Austin 100/75/50/25, All Others 600/400/200/100 (for 1, 2, 3, 4 concerts). (a) Derive demand as a public good. (b) $MC = \$425$: efficient number? (c) No fixed cost: what prices give a Lindahl equilibrium?
Givens
  • MB table by person and quantity; public good $\Rightarrow$ vertical sum $=$ add the COLUMNS
  • $MC = \$425$ constant, no fixed cost
(a) Sum each column
$$SMB(1) = 975 \quad SMB(2) = 700 \quad SMB(3) = 425 \quad SMB(4) = 250$$ Read as a (step) demand curve: society buys the $n$-th concert whenever $P \le SMB(n)$.
(b) Samuelson
At $Q = 3$: $SMB = 425 = MC$. Efficient number $= 3$ concerts.
(c) Lindahl: everyone pays their own MB at $Q^* = 3$
Per-concert prices $= MB_i(3)$: Olive 100, Peter 75, Austin 50, Others 200 (sum $= 425 = MC$). With constant $MC$, total payments are $Q^* \times MB_i$: $$\text{Olive } 300, \quad \text{Peter } 225, \quad \text{Austin } 150, \quad \text{Others } 600 \qquad (300+225+150+600 = 1275 = 425 \times 3)$$
Answer (a) steps 975, 700, 425, 250; (b) 3 concerts; (c) Lindahl payments 300 / 225 / 150 / 600
PS1 5

Picnic area: Lindahl vs the president acting alone

President's $MB = \tfrac{5}{4G}$, everyone else's $MB = \tfrac{59}{4G}$, $MC = G$. (a) Pareto-efficient size? (b) Lindahl prices? (c) Size if the president decides alone? (d) Is that efficient, and how could the local government fix it?
Givens
  • $MB_{pres} = \tfrac{5}{4G}$, $MB_{rest} = \tfrac{59}{4G}$, $MC = G$
(a) Samuelson
$$\frac{5}{4G} + \frac{59}{4G} = \frac{64}{4G} = \frac{16}{G} = G \quad\Rightarrow\quad G^2 = 16 \quad\Rightarrow\quad G^* = 4$$
(b) Lindahl prices: each pays own MB at $G^* = 4$
$$p_{pres} = \frac{5}{16} = 0.3125 \qquad p_{rest} = \frac{59}{16} = 3.6875 \qquad p_{pres} + p_{rest} = 4 = MC(4) \checkmark$$
(c) President alone: own MB $=$ MC
$$\frac{5}{4G} = G \Rightarrow G^2 = \frac54 \Rightarrow G = \frac{\sqrt 5}{2} \approx 1.1180$$
(d) Underprovision and the fix
$1.12 \ll 4$: he ignores everyone else's benefit (a positive externality), so the area is too small. The government can induce $G^* = 4$ with a matching grant / per-unit subsidy of $\tfrac{59}{4G}$ (the others' MB) so his private optimum solves $\tfrac{5}{4G} + s = MC$, or by charging Lindahl prices directly.
Answer (a) $G^* = 4$; (b) $\tfrac{5}{16}$ and $\tfrac{59}{16}$; (c) $\approx 1.118$; (d) inefficient, fix with a Pigouvian subsidy or Lindahl pricing

PS1 warm-up: the Edgeworth box split

PS1 2: authorities hand Andrea and Ben exactly half the lettuce and half the peppers. That 50/50 point is Pareto efficient only if the two indifference curves happen to be tangent there ($MRS_A = MRS_B$). With different preferences they generically CROSS at the midpoint, opening a lens of mutually beneficial trades: both can gain by swapping toward their preferred good, so the equal split is unlikely to be efficient. PS1 2

Common exam traps.

  • Aggregating the wrong direction. Adding $P$'s for a private good or $Q$'s for a public good is the classic zero. Classify FIRST, in writing: "fee + crowded $\Rightarrow$ private $\Rightarrow$ horizontal."
  • Adding demands without inverting. For the public good you must add $P_x(Q) + P_y(Q)$, not $Q_x + Q_y$. Invert before you add.
  • Forgetting the kink. Above a person's choke price they drop out of a horizontal sum. State the range.
  • Lindahl sanity check. Personalized prices must sum to $MC$ at $Q^*$. If they do not, you plugged in the wrong quantity.

Exam framing: how a full-credit MT 2 answer reads.

"A fee makes the park excludable and crowding makes it rival, so it is a private good and demands aggregate horizontally: $Q = Q_x + Q_y = 400 - 6P$ (for $P \le 50$; only X buys between 50 and 100)." Three sentences: classify with the clues, name the aggregation rule, show the algebra. The key's answers are exactly this shape.

2

Economies of scale, community size, and the decentralization theorem

This tab is the "who should provide it" toolkit: when bigger towns are cheaper per head, what the optimal size is, and exactly when the decentralization theorem does (and does not) apply. MT 1a lives here.

Play first

Find the cheapest town size

PS2's cost function $TC = NG^2 + N(4-N)^2 G$ gives per-person cost $G^2 + (4-N)^2 G$. With $G = 1$, drag $N$ and watch the per-person bill.

PS2 2

Optimal community size, then Samuelson with MRS

$U_o = 2G + 2x_o$ (old), $U_y = 6G + 2x_y$ (young); private-good $MC = 1$; producing $G$ costs $NG^2 + N(4-N)^2 G$ for a community of $N$ residents; taxes split total cost equally. (a) Show the optimal community size is 4. (b) With 2 old and 2 young residents, find the Pareto-efficient $G$.
Givens
  • $TC(N, G) = NG^2 + N(4-N)^2 G$; equal cost shares
  • $MRS = MU_G / MU_x$ (hint from the problem)
(a) Per-person cost and its minimum
$$AC(N) = \frac{TC}{N} = G^2 + (4-N)^2 G$$ For any $G > 0$ this is smallest when $(4-N)^2 = 0$, i.e. $N^* = 4$ (FOC: $\partial AC/\partial N = -2(4-N)G = 0$). That is the class definition of optimal size: the $N$ that provides the good most cheaply per resident.
(b) Samuelson with MRS, at $N = 4$
$$MRS_{old} = \frac{2}{2} = 1 \qquad MRS_{young} = \frac{6}{2} = 3 \qquad \sum MRS = 2(1) + 2(3) = 8$$ At $N = 4$: $TC = 4G^2$, so $MC_G = 8G$ (in units of the private good, whose $MC$ is 1). $$8 = 8G \quad\Rightarrow\quad G^* = 1$$
Answer (a) $N^* = 4$; (b) $G^* = 1$

Centralize or decentralize? The five-item checklist (TA session)

FactorPushes towardWhy
Variety in demandDecentralizeLocal governments tailor service levels; Tiebout: each town is a bundle of goods with prices
MobilityEitherMobile tax base argues for central collection; but mobile residents can "vote with their feet," which makes decentralized menus work
Externalities / spilloversCentralizePollution or highways cross borders; someone must account for the spillover
Economies of scaleCentralize (or contract)Bigger operations cheaper per unit
Admin and compliance costsCentralize when highOne system beats fifty

Decentralization theorem (Oates, Fiscal Federalism). For a local public good with no economies of scale (and no spillovers), it is always weakly more efficient for local governments to provide the Pareto-efficient level for their own jurisdiction than for the central government to impose any single uniform level everywhere; strictly better when preferences differ across jurisdictions. TA p. 2

MT 1a

T/F: scale study says provide at 1 million?

"A study shows no economies of scale in public broadcasting once the sharing group exceeds 1 million. Hence the decentralization theorem indicates public broadcasting should be provided by subnational governments with 1 million residents." True or false?
Givens
  • The study speaks ONLY to scale economies (the cost side)
  • Key's answer: discuss the other factors that determine optimal size
False, for two separate reasons
(1) The decentralization theorem's case for local provision rests on heterogeneous preferences and the absence of spillovers; the study establishes neither, and broadcasting is a textbook spillover (signals cross borders). (2) Finding the group size where scale economies are exhausted is a club-theory / optimal-community-size argument, not the decentralization theorem; the theorem does not prescribe a jurisdiction size at all.
Answer False: exhausting economies of scale does not invoke the theorem; spillovers and preference heterogeneity (the theorem's actual conditions) are unaddressed
MT 5

Top five revenue sources, state and local

What are the top five revenue sources for state and local governments?
The five (from the PS1 state fiscal brief research)
  1. Intergovernmental transfers (federal grants to states and localities)
  2. Property taxes (the workhorse of LOCAL government, school finance in particular)
  3. Sales and gross receipts taxes (general plus selective, like fuel and tobacco)
  4. Individual income taxes (mostly state-level)
  5. Charges and user fees (tuition, hospitals, utilities, tolls)
If your lecture slides rank them in a specific order, use that order; the five categories are the point.
Answer Federal transfers, property taxes, sales taxes, individual income taxes, charges and fees

Common exam traps.

  • The MT 1a bait. "No economies of scale past size $X$" does NOT mean "the decentralization theorem says provide at size $X$." The theorem needs no-spillovers + preference arguments; optimal size comes from minimizing $AC(n)$. Keep the two ideas in separate sentences.
  • MRS vs MB. With utility functions, Samuelson is $\sum MRS = MC_G$; compute $MRS = MU_G/MU_x$, do not invent a demand curve.
  • Equal shares are not Lindahl. Splitting cost equally is the taxation RULE in these problems; Lindahl prices are personalized and generally unequal.

Exam framing: T/F questions.

"No credit without explanation" means every T/F needs: the verdict, the correct statement of the theorem or mechanism, and the specific mismatch. One sentence each. MT 1a full credit: "False. The theorem requires no spillovers and gains from matching heterogeneous preferences; a scale study addresses neither, and broadcasting spills across borders."

3

Property taxes, Tiebout sorting, and capitalization

The school-district problem (MT 3) is the heart of this midterm: 29 points. The storyline: zoning makes the property tax a benefit tax; removing zoning invites free riding; capitalization re-prices the houses until the free ride is gone. Hold that arc and every part falls out.

Play first

Capitalization calculator

Price of a house in the mixed district solves $P + \tfrac{tP}{r} = V + \tfrac{T_{home}}{r}$ (equal total cost with the home district). Defaults reproduce MT 3e exactly.

MT 1b

T/F: higher property tax raises house prices?

"If capitalization takes place, then a higher property tax will lead to an increase in house prices to reflect the increase in cost of house ownership." True or false?
False: the sign is backwards
Capitalization means the price equals the present value of what the house delivers, $P = V + \tfrac{G - T}{r}$. A higher tax with services fixed shrinks every year's net benefit, so buyers pay LESS: higher tax costs reduce the demand for houses and the price falls. The statement treats the tax as if it were added to the price; capitalization subtracts it.
Answer False: a higher property tax is capitalized into LOWER house prices

The two districts, before anything changes

District ADistrict B
House value\$500,000\$200,000
Tax rate4%3.5%
Tax paid $=$ schools received\$20,000\$7,000

One pupil per identical house: what each family pays IS what its pupil gets. That pay $=$ get property is the benefit-tax logic that parts (a) through (g) poke at.

MT 3a

Zoning in place: move to a big house in A?

With zoning (all houses in a district the same size), would a family in district B prefer to live in a big house in district A?
No: revealed preference
Both bundles are fairly priced: pay \$7,000 for \$7,000 schools in B, or pay \$20,000 for \$20,000 schools in A. The A bundle was always available, and the family chose B; if they preferred the big-house-good-schools package they would already live there (the key's exact argument). Zoning means there is no way to get A's schools without paying A's full price, so there is no fiscal gain to moving.
Answer No: with zoning the tax is a benefit tax, and their current choice reveals their preference
MT 3b

No zoning: small house in A? (the key's subtle answer)

Suppose there is no zoning. Would a family in district B prefer to live in a small house in district A?
Read the key carefully
  • The tempting answer is "yes, free-ride!" The key's answer is cannot be determined.
Why it cannot be determined
A small house in A pays $0.04 \times 200{,}000 = \$8{,}000$ for schools spending near \$20,000: a fiscal INCENTIVE exists (the textbook's L-type family owning a below-average house in a high-service community). But whether the family actually prefers to move depends on preferences we are not given: how they trade off housing against education and other consumption. B's bundle (\$7,000 tax, \$7,000 schools) might still beat A's (\$8,000 tax, \$20,000 schools) for a family that cares little about education spending.
The bigger point (key's aside)
This is the potential instability of the Tiebout model: unless demand for the public service AND for housing are the same for everyone, mixed incentives appear. Parts (c) onward close the loophole by making everyone's desired spending identical.
Answer Cannot be determined from the information given: the incentive exists, but moving is not guaranteed without knowing preferences
MT 3c

Everyone wants \$20,000 schools; B taxes 10%

Now every family's desired education spending is \$20,000 per pupil and district B raises its tax to 10%. Would a family in B prefer a small house in district A?
Yes: now it is a pure price comparison
Both districts now deliver exactly what the family wants (\$20,000 per pupil: B at $0.10 \times 200{,}000$, A at $0.04 \times 500{,}000$). The house is the same \$200,000 either way. The only difference is the tax rate on it: 10% in B (\$20,000) vs 4% in A (\$8,000). Education identical, house identical, \$12,000 a year cheaper: the free-ride incentive, now unambiguous because preferences no longer matter.
Answer Yes: same schools, same house, \$8,000 of tax instead of \$20,000
MT 3d

Third district, 2:1 big to small: required tax rate

A third district has twice as many big houses as small houses. What tax rate spends \$20,000 per pupil?
Givens
  • Big \$500,000 ($2N$ of them), small \$200,000 ($N$), one pupil per house
  • Target: $\$20{,}000$ per pupil
Tax the average house value
$$\bar V = \frac{2N(500{,}000) + N(200{,}000)}{3N} = \frac{1{,}200{,}000}{3} = 400{,}000 \qquad t = \frac{20{,}000}{400{,}000} = 5\%$$
Verify
Revenue $= 0.05 \times 1{,}200{,}000N = 60{,}000N$; need $= 20{,}000 \times 3N = 60{,}000N$. ✓ Note the built-in cross-subsidy: big houses pay \$25,000 for \$20,000 of schooling; small houses pay \$10,000.
Answer $t = 5\%$
Variation · try it yourself
Same two house types, but big and small houses in EQUAL numbers, spending target \$21,000. Required rate?
Average value
$\bar V = \tfrac{500 + 200}{2} = 350$k, so $t = \tfrac{21{,}000}{350{,}000} = 6\%$.
MT 3e

Complete capitalization: the new prices

With complete capitalization in the third district and a 5% discount rate, what are the house prices?
Givens
  • Everyone must be indifferent between the same house type across districts (schools are \$20,000 everywhere, so only COSTS need comparing)
  • Total cost of owning $=$ price $+$ PV of taxes $=$ $P + \tfrac{t P}{r}$; the tax is 5% OF THE MARKET PRICE
  • $r = 5\%$
Big house: mixed district vs district A
$$\underbrace{500{,}000 + \frac{20{,}000}{0.05}}_{\text{cost in A} \ = \ 900{,}000} = P_{BH} + \frac{0.05\, P_{BH}}{0.05} = 2P_{BH} \quad\Rightarrow\quad P_{BH} = 450{,}000$$
Small house: mixed district vs district B
$$200{,}000 + \frac{0.10 \times 200{,}000}{0.05} = 600{,}000 = 2P_{SH} \quad\Rightarrow\quad P_{SH} = 300{,}000$$
Interpret
The small house carries a \$100,000 PREMIUM over its \$200k twin in B: it pays $0.05 \times 300{,}000 = \$15{,}000$ of tax for \$20,000 of schools, a $+\$5{,}000$/yr deal, and $\tfrac{5{,}000}{0.05} = 100{,}000$. The big house trades at a \$50,000 DISCOUNT: it pays \$22,500 for \$20,000, a $-\$2{,}500$/yr burden, and $\tfrac{2{,}500}{0.05} = 50{,}000$. The free ride is pre-sold in the price. Budget still balances: average price $\tfrac{2(450) + 300}{3} = 400$k, and $5\%$ of that is \$20,000. ✓
Answer $P_{BH} = \$450{,}000$, $P_{SH} = \$300{,}000$
Variation · try it yourself
Spending target \$24,000 everywhere; A is all \$600k houses at 4%; B is all \$200k houses at 12%; the mixed district has equal numbers of both (tax rate from the previous variation logic: $t = 24{,}000 / 400{,}000 = 6\%$). Discount rate $r = 6\%$. Prices in the mixed district?
Same two equations
Big: $600{,}000 + \tfrac{24{,}000}{0.06} = 1{,}000{,}000 = P + \tfrac{0.06P}{0.06} = 2P \Rightarrow P_{BH} = 500{,}000$. Small: $200{,}000 + \tfrac{24{,}000}{0.06} = 600{,}000 = 2P \Rightarrow P_{SH} = 300{,}000$.
Check
Average price $= 400$k; $6\%$ of it $= \$24{,}000$. ✓
MT 3f

The equilibrium with all three districts

Characterize the equilibrium that lets all three districts exist simultaneously. Support with numbers.
State every number (this is what "support with numbers" means)
All three districts spend \$20,000 per pupil. Tax rates: A $= 4\%$, B $= 10\%$, mixed $= 5\%$. Prices: big houses \$500,000 in A and \$450,000 in the mixed district; small houses \$200,000 in B and \$300,000 in the mixed district; the mixed district is 2/3 big, 1/3 small.
Why nobody moves
Total cost of a big house is the same everywhere: $500 + \tfrac{20}{0.05}\cdot\tfrac{1}{1000} \to 900$k in A and $450 + 450 = 900$k mixed. Total cost of a small house: $200 + 400 = 600$k in B and $300 + 300 = 600$k mixed. Identical schools at identical total cost: every fiscal differential is fully capitalized, so no household gains by moving and all three districts coexist.
Answer \$20k spending everywhere; rates 4 / 10 / 5 percent; prices 500 / 200 / 450 / 300 thousand; big costs \$900k and small costs \$600k in total everywhere
MT 3g

Hamilton 1975: why capitalization saves communities

Hamilton concluded that fully resolving the free-rider problem with property-tax finance requires MORE communities than the original Tiebout model. Explain why this need not be the case if capitalization occurs.
The answer in one paragraph
Without capitalization, the only way to stop free riding is zoning: a separate homogeneous community for every house-type and spending combination, hence MORE communities than Tiebout's preference-sorting alone. With capitalization, the free ride is priced instead of zoned away: the small house in a mixed district costs \$300,000, not \$200,000, so there is no incentive to move into a district where the average resident spends more than you. Mixed districts are stable, and no extra zoned communities are needed.
Answer Capitalized prices (the \$100k premium / \$50k discount) remove the free-rider incentive inside mixed districts, so communities per preference profile are unnecessary

Common exam traps.

  • The capitalization sign (MT 1b). Higher tax, fixed services $\Rightarrow$ LOWER price. If your answer has prices rising "to reflect higher cost," flip it.
  • Part (b) is not part (c). Without the \$20,000-for-everyone assumption, the key wants "cannot be determined": the incentive exists but preferences are unknown. Save the confident "yes" for (c), where preferences are pinned down.
  • Tax the market price, not the structural value. In (e), the mixed district's tax is $0.05 P$, which puts $P$ on both sides; forgetting this gives \$400k/\$400k instead of the key's \$450k/\$300k.
  • "Support with numbers" is literal. Part (f) credit comes from listing the spending, all three tax rates, all four prices, and the equal total costs.

Exam framing: the indifference template.

For any "what price makes districts coexist" question, write: $\text{price}_1 + \tfrac{\text{annual tax}_1}{r} = \text{price}_2 + \tfrac{\text{annual tax}_2}{r}$, cancel the identical service benefits, note the unknown price appears inside its own tax bill, solve. Then verify: the district budget at the new average price still funds the target spending.

4

Welfare loss and district division (Barzel's toolkit)

MT 4 is 24 points of mechanical, learnable procedure: desired quantities at the common price, the population-weighted average, the Samuelson check, and the proposal comparison. The TA session built the toolkit; the key applies it. Drag the dial below to feel why the average wins.

Play first

Minimize the county's welfare loss

MT 4's county at equal shares ($P = 2$): desired quantities $2, -1, 5$ with populations $5, 10, 10$ and $\Delta W_i = \tfrac{(Q_i - Q_0)^2}{4}$. Drag $Q_0$ and watch total loss; the curve is computed from the real formula.

Barzel's toolkit (TA session, pp. 3 to 4). For linear demand $Q_i = a_i + b_i P$ with $b_i < 0$: welfare from getting $Q$ at price $P_0$ is the trapezoid $\int_0^Q P_i(x)dx - P_0 Q$; forcing $Q_0$ instead of the desired $Q_i(P_0)$ loses the triangle $$\Delta W_i = \tfrac12\,(Q_i - Q_0)\,(P_i(Q_0) - P_0) = \frac{(Q_i - Q_0)^2}{2|b_i|}$$ and with everyone sharing one slope, the loss-minimizing uniform quantity is the population-weighted average $Q^* = \tfrac{1}{n}\sum_i Q_i(P_0)$. TA p. 3, 4

MT 4a

Desired quantities at type-specific prices

$Q_1 = 6 - 2P$, $Q_2 = 3 - 2P$, $Q_3 = 9 - 2P$; 5 type-1, 10 type-2, 10 type-3. The county charges type 1 \$2 per unit, type 2 \$1, type 3 \$3. Desired level of each type?
Plug each price into its own demand
$$Q_1 = 6 - 2(2) = 2 \qquad Q_2 = 3 - 2(1) = 1 \qquad Q_3 = 9 - 2(3) = 3$$
Answer $2, 1, 3$
MT 4b

The loss-minimizing county-wide level

Find the level of public good that minimizes total welfare loss in the county.
Givens
  • All slopes equal ($b = -2$) $\Rightarrow$ averaging rule applies
  • Desired quantities from (a): $2, 1, 3$; populations $5, 10, 10$
Population-weighted average
$$Q^* = \frac{5(2) + 10(1) + 10(3)}{25} = \frac{50}{25} = 2$$
Answer $Q^* = 2$
MT 4c

Is $Q = 2$ Pareto efficient? (Samuelson check)

Is the level in part (b) Pareto efficient? Show your work.
Givens
  • Total $MC$ $=$ sum of everyone's per-unit payments: $2(5) + 1(10) + 3(10) = 50$
  • $MB_i(Q) = \tfrac{a_i - Q}{2}$ from $Q = a_i - 2P$
Marginal benefits at $Q = 2$, weighted by population
$$MB_1 = \tfrac{6-2}{2} = 2 \qquad MB_2 = \tfrac{3-2}{2} = \tfrac12 \qquad MB_3 = \tfrac{9-2}{2} = \tfrac72$$ $$\sum_i MB_i = 5(2) + 10(\tfrac12) + 10(\tfrac72) = 10 + 5 + 35 = 50 = MC \ \checkmark$$
Answer Yes: the Samuelson condition holds at $Q = 2$, so the loss-minimizing level is Pareto efficient
MT 4d

Which redistricting proposal wins?

Residents now pay EQUALLY. Proposal 1: District I $= \{$type 1$\}$, District II $= \{$types 2, 3$\}$. Proposal 2: District I $= \{$types 1, 2$\}$, District II $= \{$type 3$\}$. Which minimizes total welfare loss?
Givens
  • Equal shares: $P = \tfrac{50}{25} = 2$ for everyone
  • Desired at $P = 2$: $Q_1 = 2$, $Q_2 = 3 - 4 = -1$ (keep it!), $Q_3 = 9 - 4 = 5$
  • Loss coefficient $\tfrac{1}{2|b|} = \tfrac14$; each district provides its own weighted average
Proposal 1: $\{1\}$ and $\{2, 3\}$
$$Q_{D1} = 2 \qquad Q_{D2} = \frac{10(-1) + 10(5)}{20} = 2$$ $$DWL_1 = 5\frac{(2-2)^2}{4} + 10\frac{(-1-2)^2}{4} + 10\frac{(5-2)^2}{4} = 0 + 22.5 + 22.5 = 45$$
Proposal 2: $\{1, 2\}$ and $\{3\}$
$$Q_{D1} = \frac{5(2) + 10(-1)}{15} = 0 \qquad Q_{D2} = 5$$ $$DWL_2 = 5\frac{(2-0)^2}{4} + 10\frac{(-1-0)^2}{4} + 10\frac{(5-5)^2}{4} = 5 + 2.5 + 0 = 7.5$$
Answer $DWL_1 = 45 > 7.5 = DWL_2$: Proposal 2 (types 1 and 2 together, type 3 alone) is better
MT 4e

The intuition, in words

Explain in words the intuition behind your findings in part (d).
Group similar demands together
Welfare loss grows with the SQUARED distance between what you want and what your district provides. Types 1 and 2 want similar amounts ($2$ and $-1$) while type 3 is the outlier ($5$). Proposal 2 puts the similar types together and gives the outlier its own district, so everyone sits close to their district's level. Proposal 1 instead traps the two most different types (2 and 3) in one district whose average ($2$) is far from both. Decentralization pays exactly when it lets jurisdictions match heterogeneous preferences: Tiebout sorting in miniature.
Answer Minimize within-district preference spread: similar types share, outliers get their own district
PS2 5

Same county, equal shares from the start

Same three demands and populations; $MC = \$25$ shared equally. (a) Desired levels? (b) Loss-minimizing level? (c) Pareto efficient? (d) Same two proposals: which is better?
(a) Common price
$P = \tfrac{25}{25} = 1$, so $Q_1 = 4$, $Q_2 = 1$, $Q_3 = 7$.
(b) Weighted average
$Q^* = \tfrac{5(4) + 10(1) + 10(7)}{25} = \tfrac{100}{25} = 4$.
(c) Samuelson
$MB_1 = 1$, $MB_2 = -\tfrac12$, $MB_3 = \tfrac52$ at $Q = 4$; weighted sum $= 5 - 5 + 25 = 25 = MC$. ✓ (A negative MB is fine: type 2 is past their satiation point.)
(d) Proposals
P1: $\{1\}$: $Q = 4$; $\{2,3\}$: $\tfrac{10(1)+10(7)}{20} = 4$; $DWL = 0 + 10\tfrac{9}{4} + 10\tfrac{9}{4} = 45$. P2: $\{1,2\}$: $\tfrac{5(4)+10(1)}{15} = 2$; $\{3\}$: $7$; $DWL = 5\tfrac{4}{4} + 10\tfrac{1}{4} + 0 = 7.5$. Proposal 2 again.
Answer (a) $4, 1, 7$; (b) $Q^* = 4$; (c) yes, $25 = 25$; (d) Proposal 2, $7.5$ vs $45$
TA ex.

Four types, two splits (TA session exercise)

$Q_1 = 5 - 3P$, $Q_2 = 8 - 3P$, $Q_3 = 9 - 3P$, $Q_4 = 6 - 3P$; 12 of each type; constant $MC = 32$ shared equally by all 48. (a) Desired levels? (b) Social planner's optimum? (c) Pareto efficient? (d) Compare districts $\{1,2\} / \{3,4\}$ vs $\{1,3\} / \{2,4\}$.
(a) Price and desired levels
$P = \tfrac{32}{48} = \tfrac23$: $Q_1 = 3$, $Q_2 = 6$, $Q_3 = 7$, $Q_4 = 4$.
(b) Average
$Q^* = \tfrac{3+6+7+4}{4} = 5$ (equal populations, so a plain mean).
(c) Samuelson
$MB_i = \tfrac{a_i - 5}{3}$: $0, 1, \tfrac43, \tfrac13$; $12(0 + 1 + \tfrac43 + \tfrac13) = 32 = MC$. ✓
(d) Two splits, coefficient $\tfrac{1}{2|b|} = \tfrac16$
Case 1 $\{1,2\},\{3,4\}$: $Q_{D1} = \tfrac92$, $Q_{D2} = \tfrac{11}{2}$; $\Delta W_1 = 12\left[\tfrac16(3-\tfrac92)^2 + \tfrac16(6-\tfrac92)^2 + \tfrac16(7-\tfrac{11}{2})^2 + \tfrac16(4-\tfrac{11}{2})^2\right] = 18$. Case 2 $\{1,3\},\{2,4\}$: both districts average $5$; $\Delta W_2 = 12\left[\tfrac16(4 + 1 + 4 + 1)\right] = 20$. Case 1 wins, $18 < 20$.
Answer (a) $3,6,7,4$; (b) $5$; (c) yes; (d) $\{1,2\}/\{3,4\}$ wins, $18 < 20$: the squared penalty punishes the big gap, so avoid pairing the extremes ($3$ with $7$)

Common exam traps.

  • Dropping the population weights. Every average and every $DWL$ sum carries the $5, 10, 10$ (or $12$s). The TA solution literally bolds this.
  • Zeroing out negative demands. $Q_2 = -1$ stays $-1$ in the average and in the loss terms. Setting it to zero changes every answer downstream.
  • Wrong coefficient. $\tfrac{1}{2|b|}$ is $\tfrac14$ when $b = -2$ (midterm) but $\tfrac16$ when $b = -3$ (TA exercise). Read the slope.
  • Using the type-specific prices in part (d). Once the question says "pays the same amount," recompute desired quantities at the COMMON price first.

Exam framing: the five-step districting answer.

(1) Common price $P = MC/\text{heads}$. (2) Desired $Q_i$ per type at that price. (3) Each district's level $=$ its weighted average. (4) $DWL = \sum n_t \tfrac{(Q_t - Q_D)^2}{2|b|}$ per proposal. (5) Compare and give the intuition sentence: "the better split groups similar demands." Write the five numbers; the points follow the procedure.

5

Mock Midterm: 5 questions, fresh numbers

Same structure as the old midterm, new numbers. Set a timer for 60 minutes, put the sheet away, and work on paper. Remember the exam's own rule: no credit without explanation. Then open the solutions and grade yourself honestly.

#1

True or false, with full justification

(a) "A study finds large economies of scale in water treatment up to 5 million users. Hence the decentralization theorem says water treatment should be provided by the central government." (b) "If complete capitalization takes place, a town that CUTS its property tax while holding services fixed will see its house prices rise."
(a) False
Economies of scale are a reason to centralize on the COST side, but the decentralization theorem is not the argument that says so: the theorem states when decentralization is (weakly) better, under no spillovers and no scale economies. With scale economies its conditions fail, so it is silent; the correct cite is the centralize-vs-decentralize checklist, not the theorem. (Same trap as MT 1a, mirrored.)
(b) True
Capitalization: $P = V + \tfrac{G - T}{r}$. Lower $T$ with $G$ fixed raises every year's net benefit, and buyers bid the PV of the savings into the price. This is MT 1b with the sign flipped: taxes down, prices up.
#2

A community pool

Two residents have inverse demand curves $Q_a = 120 - 2P_a$ and $Q_b = 120 - 3P_b$ for a community pool. (a) Everyone pays to swim and the pool is packed: aggregate demand? (b) Free entry and the pool is nearly deserted: aggregate demand?
(a) Private (fee + packed): horizontal
$$Q = (120 - 2P) + (120 - 3P) = 240 - 5P \text{ for } P \le 40; \qquad Q = 120 - 2P \text{ for } 40 < P \le 60$$ (B's choke price is 40, A's is 60.)
(b) Public (free + empty): vertical
Invert: $P_a = 60 - \tfrac12 Q$, $P_b = 40 - \tfrac13 Q$. $$P = 100 - \tfrac56 Q$$ Both individual curves hit zero at $Q = 120$, so no kink on the relevant range.
#3

School districts, remixed

District A: all \$600,000 houses, tax 4%. District B: all \$200,000 houses, tax 12%. Every family wants \$24,000 per pupil (both districts deliver it; one pupil per house). (a) A third district has big and small houses in EQUAL numbers: what tax rate funds \$24,000 per pupil? (b) With complete capitalization and a 6% discount rate, find the third district's house prices. (c) Verify no one wants to move.
(a) Average value
$$\bar V = \tfrac{600{,}000 + 200{,}000}{2} = 400{,}000 \qquad t = \tfrac{24{,}000}{400{,}000} = 6\%$$
(b) Indifference, tax on the market price, $t = r = 6\%$
Big vs A: $600{,}000 + \tfrac{0.04 \times 600{,}000}{0.06} = 600{,}000 + 400{,}000 = 1{,}000{,}000 = 2P_{BH}$, so $P_{BH} = \$500{,}000$. Small vs B: $200{,}000 + \tfrac{0.12 \times 200{,}000}{0.06} = 200{,}000 + 400{,}000 = 600{,}000 = 2P_{SH}$, so $P_{SH} = \$300{,}000$.
(c) Check totals and the budget
Big house total cost: \$1,000,000 in A and $500 + \tfrac{0.06 \times 500}{0.06} = 1{,}000$ thousand in the mixed district. Small: \$600,000 both places. Budget: average price $= \tfrac{500 + 300}{2} = 400$k and $6\% \times 400{,}000 = \$24{,}000$ per pupil. ✓ No fiscal gain anywhere: equilibrium.
#4

Welfare loss and redistricting

Three types: $Q_1 = 8 - 2P$, $Q_2 = 4 - 2P$, $Q_3 = 12 - 2P$; 5 type-1, 10 type-2, 10 type-3 residents. Total marginal cost \$50, shared equally. (a) Desired level of each type? (b) County-wide level minimizing total welfare loss? (c) Is it Pareto efficient? (d) Proposal 1: $\{1\}$ and $\{2,3\}$; Proposal 2: $\{1,2\}$ and $\{3\}$. Which is better? (e) Intuition?
(a) Common price
$P = \tfrac{50}{25} = 2$: $Q_1 = 4$, $Q_2 = 0$, $Q_3 = 8$.
(b) Weighted average
$Q^* = \tfrac{5(4) + 10(0) + 10(8)}{25} = \tfrac{100}{25} = 4$.
(c) Samuelson
$MB$ at 4: $\tfrac{8-4}{2} = 2$, $\tfrac{4-4}{2} = 0$, $\tfrac{12-4}{2} = 4$; weighted: $5(2) + 10(0) + 10(4) = 50 = MC$. ✓ Efficient.
(d) Compare (coefficient $\tfrac14$)
P1: $\{1\}$ provides 4; $\{2,3\}$ provides $\tfrac{10(0) + 10(8)}{20} = 4$; $DWL_1 = 0 + 10\tfrac{16}{4} + 10\tfrac{16}{4} = 80$. P2: $\{1,2\}$ provides $\tfrac{5(4) + 10(0)}{15} = \tfrac43$; $\{3\}$ provides 8; $DWL_2 = 5\tfrac{(4 - 4/3)^2}{4} + 10\tfrac{(0 - 4/3)^2}{4} + 0 = \tfrac{80}{9} + \tfrac{40}{9} = \tfrac{120}{9} \approx 13.33$. Proposal 2 wins.
(e) Intuition
Type 3 is the outlier (wants 8); giving it its own district and grouping the similar types 1 and 2 keeps everyone near their district's level. Squared losses punish the big mismatches hardest.
#5

Short answer

(a) State the decentralization theorem, including its conditions. (b) List the top five revenue sources for state and local governments.
(a)
For a local public good with no economies of scale and no inter-jurisdictional spillovers, it is always at least as efficient (weakly more efficient) for local governments to provide the Pareto-efficient output for their own jurisdictions than for the central government to provide any uniform level everywhere; strictly more efficient when preferences differ across jurisdictions. (Oates, Fiscal Federalism.)
(b)
Intergovernmental transfers from the federal government; property taxes; sales and gross receipts taxes; individual income taxes; charges and user fees.
